accroche: In July 1793, the National Convention passes a text that gives authors an exclusive right to sell their own works.
contenu_vulgarise:
Paris, July 19, 1793. The National Convention sits in an unstable political climate, a few weeks after the Girondins were eliminated in June 1793, and yet it passes, on the report of deputy Joseph Lakanal, speaking for the public education committee, a text unrelated to the urgencies of the moment: a law concerning the property rights of authors of writings of every kind, music composers, painters and draftsmen. The text bears the signature of July 24, five days later.

## What the law grants, article by article

The first article gives the author an exclusive right to sell and distribute his work, for his entire lifetime. The second passes this right to his heirs or assigns for ten years after his death: a term that later laws would lengthen for authors' children, to twenty years in 1810 and then thirty in 1854. The third instructs the “officiers de paix” (peace officers) to seize counterfeit copies. The fourth sets the compensation owed by the infringer at the price of three thousand copies of the original edition. The sixth requires that two copies of every published work be deposited at the Bibliothèque nationale (the national library), failing which the author will not be admitted to court against infringers. In all, the law has seven articles.

The text makes no mention of the Old Regime's printing privileges, but the legal scholar Frédéric Rideau (University of Poitiers) notes that it partly takes up the choice already made by the royal decrees of August 30, 1777, a lineage Lakanal avoided mentioning. Two years earlier, in January 1791, a first law on theatrical performances had already granted living playwrights a right to have their plays performed, limited to five years after their death. The 1793 law extends the principle to writing, music and drawing.

## A property, not yet a person

This founding text is often credited with having invented, as early as 1793, what would set France apart from Anglo-American law: a “droit moral” (moral right), attached to the author's person rather than to his economic interest alone. The text itself says no such thing. Its seven articles speak only of sale, distribution, seizure, compensation and deposit: a property-based architecture that, on this specific point, resembles that of England's Copyright Act of 1710. Nothing in it provides that an author may object to the alteration of his work, claim authorship against his will, or withdraw it from circulation.

Moral rights would be born elsewhere and later: first in French case law, with the courts recognizing prerogatives for authors that the 1793 law did not give them (Frédéric Rideau's commentary dates this recognition to 1902, in the Lecocq case), then, more than a century and a half after the Convention, in the law of March 11, 1957 on literary and artistic property, which codifies these rights. What the Convention really invented in 1793 was a right of property in the work. What France would add afterward, the work of judges rather than legislators, was a right over the bond between the author and his work: a distinction the 1793 text did not yet carry.

repere.texte: The law of July 19, 1793 sets the compensation owed by an infringer at the price of three thousand copies of the original edition of the copied work, and grants the author's heirs only ten years of rights after his death, a term that the French law of April 8, 1854 would raise to thirty years for authors' children.
repere.source: Law of July 19, 1793, articles 2 and 4, and note on the law of April 8, 1854 (Wikisource)

carte.punch: French copyright is born in July 1793, and it is still only a right to sell.
carte.idee: On July 19, 1793, the National Convention passes a law giving authors an exclusive right to sell their works. The moral right often attributed to it is not in it: the courts will recognize it, and the 1957 law will codify it.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Légifrance — Law No. 57-298 of March 11, 1957 on literary and artistic property
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The text that codifies, more than a century and a half after the 1793 decree, the rights that case law had recognized for authors, including moral rights.

quiz.question: What does the decree of July 19, 1793 actually provide regarding authors' rights?
choix: A moral right allowing them to object to any alteration of their work
An exclusive right to sell and distribute, passed to their heirs for ten years after their death
A perpetual property right, transmissible without any time limit
A right reserved for writers alone, excluding musicians and painters
quiz.explication: The text is purely economic: an exclusive right to sell during the author's lifetime, passed on for ten years after death. It contains no moral-rights provision, it also applies to composers and painters, and it is not perpetual.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When is the author's moral right codified in French law?
choix: As early as the decree of July 19, 1793
By the law of March 11, 1957 on literary and artistic property, after being recognized by the courts
It has never been codified; only case law still recognizes it today
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Moral rights are first recognized by the courts, then codified by the law of March 11, 1957: more than a century and a half after the 1793 decree, which did not contain them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What formality does the 1793 decree impose for an author to be able to act against an infringement?
choix: Registering the work with the National Convention
Depositing two copies of the work at the Bibliothèque nationale
Publishing the work in the Journal officiel
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text requires two copies to be deposited at the Bibliothèque nationale, failing which the author cannot be admitted to court against infringers (article 6). The other formalities do not appear in it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which law precedes the 1793 one by already granting playwrights a right of performance?
choix: The Le Chapelier law of June 1791, banning guilds
The January 1791 law on theatrical performances, granting living authors a right of performance
The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The January 1791 law on theatrical performances already grants living playwrights a right to have their plays performed, limited to five years after their death; the 1793 law extends this principle to writing, music and drawing. The Le Chapelier law of June 1791, for its part, concerns the banning of guilds and has no connection to copyright.
